en: Now begins the instruction on yoga. YS 1.1.
Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind.
Then there is the abiding of the seer in his own true nature. (YS 1.3)
In other cases, there is conformity with the mental modifications. (YS 1.4)
The fluctuations are of five kinds, both afflicted and unafflicted.
Valid cognition, error, conceptual construction, sleep, and memory. (YS 1.6)
Perception, inference, and valid testimony are the means of valid cognition.
Error is false knowledge, which is not established in the true nature of its object.
Conceptual construction (vikalpa) is that which follows upon the knowledge of words and is devoid of a real object. (YS 1.9)
Sleep is a mental modification whose object is the notion of non-existence.
Memory is the non-loss of an experienced object.
Their cessation is achieved through practice and detachment. (YS 1.12)
In that regard, practice is the effort toward steadiness. (YS 1.13)
But that [practice], when cultivated for a long time, without interruption, and with devotion, becomes firmly established.
Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the consciousness of mastery in one who is free from thirst for objects seen or heard of in tradition. *Yoga Sūtra* 1.15.
That supreme state is dispassion toward the *guṇas*, following from the discernment of the *puruṣa*.

Cognitive absorption (*samprajñāta-samādhi*) is so called because it follows the forms of applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), bliss (*ānanda*), and the sense of self (*asmitā*).
The other [samādhi] is preceded by the practice of the causal sign of cessation and consists of residual latent impressions alone.
For those who have dissolved into the bodyless state or into primordial nature, the cause is existence itself.
For others, [the practice] is preceded by faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
It is near for those who possess intense spiritual urgency.
There is a further distinction [of progress] due to the mild, medium, and intense degrees [of practice]. (YS 1.22)
Or [samādhi is attained] through devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna). YS 1.23.
The Lord is a distinct Puruṣa, untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, or their latent dispositions.
In that state, there exists the unsurpassed seed of omniscience.
He is also the teacher of the ancients, because he is not limited by time.
The syllable *praṇava* is its designator.
The repetition of that [mantra] and the contemplation of its meaning.
From that, there arises the realization of the inward-turned consciousness as well as the absence of obstacles.
Illness, languor, doubt, heedlessness, laziness, lack of renunciation, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage, and instability—these distractions of the mind are the obstacles. (YS 1.30)
Pain, mental distress, trembling of the limbs, and irregular breathing are concomitants of distraction.
To prevent that, there is the practice of a single principle (ekatattvābhyāsa). (YS 1.32)
The clarification of the mind results from the cultivation of friendliness, compassion, joy, and equanimity toward those who are happy, suffering, virtuous, and non-virtuous, respectively.
Or [the mind becomes one-pointed] by means of exhalation and retention of the breath.
Or, when an activity of the mind directed toward an object arises, it becomes a means for stabilizing the mind.
Or it is sorrowless and luminous.
Or the mind has as its object one who is free from passion.
Or it has as its object the cognition of dreaming or deep sleep.
Or [the mind becomes one-pointed] through meditation on whatever is desired. (YS 1.39)
The mastery over this [mind] extends from the subtlest atom to the greatest magnitude.

For one whose fluctuations have ceased, there is a meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) characterized by abiding in and being colored by that [object] with respect to the grasper, the grasping, and the graspable, like a noble jewel.
Therein, the meditative attainment mixed with conceptual constructions of word, object, and knowledge is *savitarka*. (Yogasūtra 1.42)
When memory is purified, the state of samādhi in which the object alone appears as if devoid of its own specific form is called *nirvitarka*.
By this very [same explanation], the [samādhis] with deliberation (savicārā) and without deliberation (nirvicārā), which have subtle objects, are explained.
And the state of having subtle objects culminates in the unmanifest (aliṅga).
These very [attainments] are the seeded concentration (sabīja-samādhi).
When there is mastery over the state free from subtle reflection, there is inner clarity.
In that state, wisdom is truth-bearing. (YS 1.48)
It has an object different from the wisdoms derived from hearing and inference, because it pertains to specific particulars.
The impression born therefrom obstructs other impressions. (YS 1.50)
When that [citta] is also ceased, because of the cessation of everything, there is seedless samādhi.
Austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord constitute the yoga of action.
The purpose of the cultivation of meditative concentration is for the thinning of the afflictions.
Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are the afflictions.
Ignorance is the field for the subsequent [afflictions], whether they be dormant, attenuated, interrupted, or active.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the perception of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in that which is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self. (YS 2.5)
Asmitā is the apparent identity between the power of the seer and the power of seeing.
Attachment is that which lies latent within pleasure.
Aversion is that which lies latent within suffering.
The innate clinging to life flows spontaneously; it is thus deeply rooted even in the wise.
These subtle [afflictions] are to be abandoned by re-absorption.
The fluctuations of those [senses] are to be abandoned by means of meditative absorption (dhyāna).
The latent deposit of karma has its root in the afflictions; it is to be experienced in the present or future birth.
When the root exists, its fruition consists of birth, lifespan, and experience.
They have joy and sorrow as their fruits, because they have merit and demerit as their causes.
To the discerning person, all is indeed suffering because of the sufferings of change, anxiety, and latent impressions, and because of the conflict between the fluctuations of the guṇas.
Future suffering is to be abandoned.
The conjunction of the seer and the seen is the cause of that which is to be abandoned.
The object of perception consists of the elements and the sense organs, whose nature is illumination, activity, and inertia, and which exists for the purpose of experience and liberation. (YS 2.18)
The stages of the gunas are the evolved (viśeṣa), the unevolved (aviśeṣa), the mere-indicative (liṅgamātra), and the non-indicative (aliṅga).
The Seer is pure consciousness alone; though pure, it observes the mental modifications.
The very nature of the object of perception is for that [purpose]. (YS 2.21)
Although it has perished for one who has attained their purpose, it is not lost, because it is common to others.
Conjunction is the cause for the perception of the essential nature of both the self and its master [the Lord]. (YS 2.23)
Its cause is ignorance (avidyā). YS 2.24.
From the absence of that [ignorance], there is the absence of conjunction; this is liberation, the isolation of the Seer.
The means of liberation is undisturbed discriminative discernment.
His wisdom is sevenfold in its final stage.
From the practice of the limbs of yoga, upon the destruction of impurity, there arises the illumination of knowledge up to discriminative discernment.

The eight limbs are restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi). // YS 2.29 //
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the restraints (yamas).
Unrestricted by birth, place, time, or circumstance, these universal observances constitute the Great Vow.
Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances (niyamas).
When discursive thought causes affliction, one should cultivate its antidote.

For discursive thoughts such as violence and the like—whether performed, caused to be performed, or approved; whether preceded by greed, anger, or delusion; and whether mild, moderate, or intense—result in endless fruits of suffering and ignorance; thus is the cultivation of their antidote. (YS 2.34)
When non-violence is firmly established, hostility ceases in its presence.
When there is steadiness in truth, there is the attainment of the fruits of action.
When non-stealing is firmly established, all jewels present themselves.
Upon the establishment of celibacy, there is the attainment of vigor.
When non-possessiveness is firmly established, there arises a thorough understanding of the circumstances of one's births.
From purity comes disgust for one's own body and non-association with others.
And there arise purity of the mind-stuff, cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery over the senses, and fitness for the vision of the Self. (YS 2.41)
From contentment comes the attainment of unsurpassed happiness.
The perfection of the sense of touch results from the destruction of impurities through austerity.
From the study of sacred texts comes communion with one's chosen deity.
Success in samādhi comes from devotion to the Lord.
Posture is that which is firm and pleasant. (YS 2.46)
By relaxation of effort and by meditative absorption in the infinite.
From that, there is no affliction by the pairs of opposites.
When that [posture] is achieved, the cessation of the flow of inhalation and exhalation is breath control (prāṇāyāma). // YS 2.49 //
The flow of the breath, whether external or internal, regulated by place, time, and number, becomes long and subtle.
The fourth [type of breath restraint] is that which projects the objects both external and internal.
Thereupon, the veil over the light is destroyed.
And there is fitness of the mind for the dhāraṇās.
Pratyāhāra (withdrawal) is the sense organs' imitation, as it were, of the nature of the mind itself when they are not in contact with their own objects. 2.54.
Thereafter, there is supreme mastery over the senses. (YS 2.55)
Dhāraṇā (concentration) is the binding of the mind to a particular place.
Therein, meditation (dhyāna) is the one-pointed continuity of the cognition with respect to that object. (YS 3.2)
That very [samādhi] in which only the object appears, as if devoid of its own nature, is samādhi. (YS 3.3)
The three together in one place constitute *saṃyama*.
From the conquest of that [mind-stuff], there arises the light of wisdom. (YS 3.5)
Its application is to the stages [of yoga]. (YS 3.6)
The triad [of practice, observance, and posture] is more internal than the preceding ones.
Even that is external to the seedless [samādhi]. (YS 3.8)

The transformation of cessation (nirodha-pariṇāma) consists in the suppression of the latent impressions of emergence and the manifestation of the latent impressions of cessation, followed by the succession of moments of consciousness characterized by cessation.
Its state of tranquil flow arises from mental refinement.
The transformation of the mind through concentration consists in the waning of its tendency toward all objects and the arising of its one-pointedness.
Then again, the transformation of one-pointedness of the mind consists in the subsided and arisen cognitions being identical in nature.
By this, the transformations of property, characteristic, and state in the elements and the sense organs are explained.
The substrate (dharmin) conforms to attributes (dharmas) that are quiescent, emergent, or unmanifest.
The difference in sequence is the cause for the difference in transformation.
Through *saṃyama* on the three transformations, there arises knowledge of the past and the future.
Due to the mutual superimposition of word, object, and cognition, there is a confusion; by performing *saṃyama* on their distinction, knowledge of the cries of all beings arises. (YS 3.17)
Through the direct realization of the formative forces (saṃskāra), knowledge of previous births arises. (YS 3.18)
The supernormal knowledge of another's mind arises from the meditative object [of that mind]. (YS 3.19)
And that [citta] does not have an object-support, because [the other citta] has not become its object-field. (YS 3.20)
Through *saṃyama* on the form of the body, when the power of its perceptibility is suppressed and there is no contact with the light of the eye, invisibility occurs. (YS 3.21)
Action is either with onset or without onset; through *saṃyama* upon it, or from portents, there arises knowledge of the time of death.
The powers [arise] from friendliness and the other [immeasurables]. (YS 3.23)
Among the powers, there are the power of an elephant and so forth. (YS 3.24)
Through the application of the light of the outgoing [breath], there arises knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, and the distant.
Knowledge of the worlds [is attained] through *saṃyama* on the sun. (YS 3.26)
Through the moon, there is knowledge of the arrangement of the stars. (YS 3.27)
From [meditation on] the Pole Star, there arises knowledge of its motion. (YS 3.28)
Through the navel-center, there arises knowledge of the arrangement of the body. (YS 3.29)
In the throat-pit, there is the cessation of hunger and thirst. (YS 3.30)
Stability [of the mind] is attained through the *kūrma* channel. (YS 3.31)
When the light at the crown of the head is attained, there is the vision of the perfected ones (siddhas).
Or, through intuitive insight, all [is known]. (YS 3.33)
In the heart, there is the knowledge of the mind. (YS 3.34)

Experience is the non-differentiation of the cognitions of the sattva and the puruṣa, which are absolutely distinct; from saṃyama upon one's own nature as distinct from that which exists for another, there arises knowledge of the puruṣa. (YS 3.35)
From that, intuitive knowledge, the power of hearing, the power of touch, the power of sight, the power of taste, and the power of smell arise. (YS 3.36)
These are obstacles to concentration, but they are accomplishments when one has emerged from it.
Through the loosening of the cause of bondage and through the awareness of the movement of the mind, there is entry into another's body. (YS 3.38)
From mastery over the udāna breath, there is non-attachment to water, mud, thorns, and the like, as well as the power of upward departure.
From mastery over the *samāna* breath, there is radiance.
Through *saṃyama* on the connection between the ear and space, divine hearing arises. (YS 3.41)
Through *saṃyama* on the connection between the body and space, and through meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) on lightness like that of cotton, one attains the power of moving through space.
The external, non-conceptualized state of existence is the "Great Bodilessness" (mahāvideha); from that follows the destruction of the veil covering the light.
Through *saṃyama* on the gross form, the subtle nature, and the inherence [of the qualities]—that is, their purposefulness—there is mastery over the elements (*bhūta*).
From that, there arises the manifestation of the powers such as atomization (aṇimā), perfection of the body, and non-obstruction by the properties of matter.
The perfection of the body consists of beauty, grace, strength, and adamantine firmness.
Through saṃyama on the essential nature of perception, egoism, continuity, and purposefulness, mastery over the senses is attained.
From that [mastery of the five stages], there arise the power of moving with the speed of mind, the state of being without organs, and mastery over the primary cause (prakṛti).
For one who possesses the mere discriminative discernment of the difference between the sattva and the puruṣa, there arises sovereignty over all states of being and omniscience. (YS 3.49)
From detachment even toward that [subtle body], upon the destruction of the seeds of defects, there is isolation (kaivalya).
Upon being invited by those who dwell in the higher realms, one should avoid attachment and pride, for otherwise there is the risk of falling back into undesirable states.
From *saṃyama* on the moment and its sequence, knowledge born of discrimination arises.
Because difference is not delimited by genus, characteristic, or location, the cognition of two identical things arises from that [similarity].
The knowledge born of discrimination is saving, has all things as its object, has everything as its object in every way, and is beyond succession. (YS 3.54)
When there is equality of purity between the sattva and the puruṣa, there is isolation (kaivalya). // YS 3.55 //
The supernatural powers (siddhis) are born of birth, herbs, mantras, austerity, and meditative concentration.
The transformation into another species occurs through the influx of primal nature (prakṛti).
The efficient cause is not the motivator of the *prakṛtis*; rather, it serves to break through their covering, like a farmer [who provides water to a field]. (YS 4.3)
The minds of emanation arise from the mere sense of "I-am-ness."
The single mind is the motivator for the various activities of many.
Among these, that which is born of meditative absorption (dhyāna) is without latent impressions (anāśaya).
The karma of the yogi is neither white nor black; for others, it is of three kinds.
Consequently, there is the manifestation only of those latent impressions (vāsanās) that are conducive to that specific fruition.
Even for those [impressions] separated by birth, space, and time, there is immediate succession because memory and the latent impressions (saṃskāra) are of a single nature. (YS 4.9)
And their beginninglessness is due to the eternity of the desire for existence.
Because these [categories] are subsumed by cause, fruit, basis, and object, in their absence, those [categories] are absent. (YS 4.11)
The past and the future exist in their own nature, due to the distinction of the temporal paths of dharmas.
These manifest and subtle [objects] consist of the gunas.
The reality of an object consists in the unity of its transformations. (YS 4.14)
Since there is a difference in the minds even when the object is the same, the paths of these two are distinct.
And since an object does not depend solely on a single mind, what would become of that object if it were not being perceived at that time? (YS 4.16)
Because the mind depends upon its coloring by that [object], an object is either known or unknown. (YS 4.17)
The fluctuations of the mind are always known by their master, the Puruṣa, because of his unchangeability. (YS 4.18)
That [cognition] does not have itself as its own appearance, because it is an object of perception. (YS 4.19)
And at one time, there is no determination of both. (YS 4.20)
If one cognition were perceived by another cognition, there would be an infinite regress of cognitions, as well as a confusion of memories. (YS 4.21)
By means of non-transmigration [of the mind], there is the self-awareness of one's own intellect upon attaining that form. (YS 4.22)
The mind, colored by both the seer and the seen, has all things as its object.
Although that [mind] is variegated by innumerable latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it exists for the sake of another because it functions through collective action. (YS 4.24)
For one who perceives the distinction, there is the cessation of the cultivation of self-existence.
Then the mind becomes inclined toward discernment and tends toward isolation. (YS 4.26)
In those intervals, other cognitions arise from latent dispositions (saṃskāras). // YS 4.27 //
Furthermore, their [destruction] has been described as being like that of the afflictions.
For one who is even in the state of discriminative discernment free from desire for it, the samādhi called the Cloud of Virtue arises through the complete manifestation of discriminative discernment.
From that follows the cessation of afflictions and karma. (YS 4.30)
Then, because knowledge is infinite for one who is freed from all the stains of obscuration, the knowable becomes small. (YS 4.31)
Thereafter, for those whose purpose has been accomplished, there is the cessation of the sequence of the transformation of the guṇas.
Succession is the counter-correlative of the moment, and it is to be grasped by the final limit of transformation.
Isolation (kaivalya) is the reabsorption of the guṇas, which are devoid of the purposes of the Puruṣa, or it is the power of consciousness established in its own nature. (YS 4.34)
